newsitem.title: INDIA: GOOD DEMAND FOR ARABICA AT INDIAN COFFEE AUCTION.
newsitem.headline: GOOD DEMAND FOR ARABICA AT INDIAN COFFEE AUCTION.

text.p: There was good demand for Indian primary arabica varieties at this week's coffee auction in the southern city of Bangalore, auctioneers said on Friday.
"The sale witnessed good demand with primary arabica varieties gaining between three rupees and six rupees," the Karnataka Coffee Brokers Pvt Ltd, a leading auctioner said in a statement.
The company said robusta parchments rose marginally on quality while the cherry grades were steady to occasionally higher.
It said exporters were subdued while domestic dealers were selective on primary grades and active on other grades.
The company said arabica parchments peaberry was quoted at 141 rupees per kg while the prime 'A' grade was quoted at 142 rupees per kg.
Robusta parchment peaberry was quoted at 69 rupees per kg and robusta cherry full grown flat bean was traded at 70 rupees per kg.
"The internal buyers are very strong and exporters were subdued," a company official told Reuters.
He said selling was at a low level because export demand was low with Indonesia and Ivory coast selling similar brands at lesser differentials.
At this week's auction, 81.7 tonnes of arabica were sold out of 274 tonnes on offer. Nearly 98 tonnes of robustas of the 537 tonnes offered were picked up, the statement said.
India, which exports most of its coffee production, has freed the coffee trade from five-decade-old marketing controls over the past four years, allowing growers to directly market their produce.
The state-run Coffee Board earlier collected coffee from the growers and auctioned it both for domestic and export markets.
The recently-formed Indian Coffee Trade Association, representing growers, traders and exporters, now holds weekly auctions at Bangalore.

Traders estimated the 1997/98 (October/September) coffee crop at around 220,000 tonnes, up from 180,000 tonnes in the previous year. India's coffee exports in 1996/97 (April-March) rose to 178,000 tonnes from 170,000 tonnes in the previous year.
The company said between January and June 1997, India shipped 72,783 tonnes of coffee.
Indian Commerce Minister Bolla Buli Ramaiah was quoted on Tuesday as saying India did not plan to allow coffee imports as prices had come down from recent peaks.

Newsreports in June quoted the highest-ranking civil servant in the Commerce Ministry, P.P. Prabhu, as saying the government was considering permitting coffee imports to help stabilise domestic prices, which had risen sharply.
Domestic prices, tracking international prices, have since come down, helped by expectations of a bountiful Indian crop in 1997/98 (July-June).
India's early arabica coffee crop is expected to be ready by the end of November.
Indian retail coffee prices have now stabilised at around 180 rupees per kg after soaring to 220 rupees in June from 160 in the previous month, traders said.
$1 = 35.8 rupees
-- Hari Ramachandran
